title: LinkedIn Pipeline Readiness Score
subtitle: Find out whether your LinkedIn presence is actually building predictable pipeline or just collecting impressions.

questions.text: How well can you describe what your ideal client has already tried before finding you?

answers.label: I focus on their title and company size. I have not thought much beyond that.
I have a general sense but could not name specific things they have attempted.
I know a few common pain points but not the full picture of what they have tried.
I can name specific tactics or solutions they tried that did not work.
I know exactly what they tried, why it failed, and what finally made them take action.

questions.text: When you write content, how specifically do you speak to your ideal client's frustrations, not just what they want?

answers.label: My content is mostly about what I do and what I offer.
I mention pain points occasionally but mostly lead with my solution.
I address frustrations sometimes but it is not a consistent part of my strategy.
I regularly write about their specific frustrations and it connects.
My content consistently names the exact frustrations that make my ICP stop scrolling.

questions.text: How clearly do you understand what objections stop your ideal client from buying, and what finally makes them take action?

answers.label: I have not mapped this out. I respond to objections as they come up on calls.
I know a couple of common objections but have not dug into what triggers a decision.
I understand the main objections but I am fuzzy on what tips them into action.
I know both their objections and the moment they typically decide to move.
I can name every major objection and the exact trigger that makes them reach out or buy.

low.headline: Your ICP is still blurry. Your messaging shows it.
low.text: The most common reason LinkedIn content does not generate leads is not the platform. It is that you are saying the right things to the wrong picture of a person. More activity will not fix this. It just amplifies it. Before you post another thing, get clear on who you are actually talking to.
steps: Interview 3 to 5 current or past clients specifically about what they tried before finding you and why it did not work
Write a one-paragraph before-state for your ICP: their frustration, their failed attempts, the moment they knew they needed help
Read your last 10 posts and ask honestly: if I were my ideal client, would any of these make me stop scrolling?

mid.headline: You know your client. Now go a layer deeper.
mid.text: You have the foundation. But knowing your ICP's job title and general pain points is not the same as knowing what keeps getting deprioritized on their list, or what objection stops them right before they buy. That is the layer that makes content actually hit.
steps: Pick your top 2 buyer personas and write out their complete before-story: what they tried, what frustrated them, what finally made them move
Audit your content from the last 30 days. Are you speaking to their frustrations or mostly your solutions?
Add one post this week that names a specific objection you hear often and addresses it directly

high.headline: You know your buyer. That is a real advantage.
high.text: Deep ICP clarity is rare, and it shows up in content that makes people feel seen. Keep feeding this. The more real conversations you have with clients, the sharper your messaging stays.
steps: Make sure your ICP insights are making it into your content consistently, not just in occasional posts
Review your content quarterly and check whether your messaging still matches where your buyers actually are right now
Use client language verbatim in your posts when possible. The exact words your buyers use are more powerful than anything you would write from scratch.

questions.text: If you received your own cold outreach message today, how likely would you be to respond?

answers.label: Honestly? Probably not. It looks like every other message in my inbox.
Maybe. It is decent but nothing about it stands out.
I might respond if the timing was right.
Probably yes. It is relevant and speaks to something real.
Absolutely. It would stop me, feel personal, and make the next step obvious.

questions.text: How clearly does your LinkedIn profile communicate who you help and what changes for them when they work with you?

answers.label: It lists my experience and title. People have to work to figure out how I help.
It mentions what I do but does not clearly spell out who it is for or what they get.
It is clear enough but the outcome for the client is not front and center.
It is clear who I help and what the main outcome is.
Someone in my ICP would read my profile and immediately think: this is exactly for me.

questions.text: How clearly can you explain what makes your approach different from others who offer something similar?

answers.label: I know we are different but I struggle to articulate it clearly.
I can explain it but it comes out differently every time I try.
I have a positioning statement but it could be sharper.
I can explain my differentiation clearly and use it consistently.
My positioning is locked in and shows up the same way in my content, profile, and conversations.

low.headline: More activity will not fix broken messaging. It amplifies it.
low.text: Before you ask yourself how to generate more leads, ask yourself: if I were my ideal client, would I respond to my own messaging? If the honest answer is no, posting more and reaching out to more people is not the fix. Clarity is.
steps: Rewrite your LinkedIn headline to include who you help and what changes for them. Cut the generic job title language.
Send your current cold outreach message to a trusted peer and ask them honestly: would you respond to this?
Write one sentence that explains your differentiation and test it in your next three conversations

mid.headline: Your message is getting there. Tighten the specificity.
mid.text: You have the bones of strong positioning. The gap is usually specificity. Vague outcomes do not create urgency the way specific ones do. 'I help you grow' lands very differently than 'I help B2B founders book 10 qualified calls a month from LinkedIn alone.'
steps: Look at your last 5 outreach messages. Where do they get vague? Replace abstract language with concrete outcomes.
Ask 3 past clients what they would have searched for before finding you. Use their exact words in your next post.
Test two different versions of your positioning with real prospects this week and track which one generates more responses

high.headline: Sharp messaging is your biggest competitive advantage. Protect it.
high.text: When your message is dialed in, everything gets easier. Outreach lands. Content attracts the right people. Sales conversations start with the hard work already done. Stay close to your ICP so your message stays sharp as the market moves.
steps: Audit your positioning every quarter. What your buyers care about shifts, and your message should shift with it.
Make sure your messaging is consistent across your profile, content, outreach, and proposals
Build messaging into how you onboard new clients. Their language and story will keep your positioning sharp.

questions.text: What happens most often after someone reads your LinkedIn content?

answers.label: They like it or comment. It rarely leads to a conversation or a next step.
Occasionally someone reaches out, but it is unpredictable.
Some posts drive conversations but I do not have a consistent pattern.
My content regularly leads to profile visits, DMs, or lead magnet downloads.
My content reliably drives qualified conversations, inbound requests, and real pipeline activity.

questions.text: How intentional is your content strategy? Do your posts connect to a clear next step for the reader?

answers.label: I post when I have something to say. There is no real strategy behind it.
I try to post regularly but the posts do not always connect to a business outcome.
Some posts have a clear CTA or next step but it is not consistent across everything I publish.
Most of my content has a clear purpose and leads somewhere intentional.
Every post is part of a strategy. Attention earns trust, trust drives action, action builds pipeline.

questions.text: Do you have a lead magnet (guide, checklist, template, or resource) that captures interest from warm prospects?

answers.label: No. People either book a call or do nothing.
I have thought about building one but have not done it yet.
I have something but it is not getting much traction.
I have a lead magnet and it drives some downloads, though I could promote it more.
My lead magnet consistently surfaces buying intent and moves the right people into my pipeline.

questions.text: How many qualified leads does LinkedIn generate for you in a typical month?
questions.hint: Count inbound DMs, conversations from content that turned into calls, and lead magnet downloads that became real conversations. A consistent LinkedIn system generates 10 or more qualified conversations per month.

low.headline: Attention without a next step is a dead end.
low.text: A post with 100,000 impressions and no next step might make your ego feel great, but it does not build a pipeline. If your content is getting attention but not driving real conversations, you are missing the bridge. That bridge is a clear next step that gives buyers somewhere to go when they are ready.
steps: Audit your last 10 posts: does each one have a clear next step? A lead magnet, a DM prompt, a profile worth visiting?
Build one lead magnet this month that solves a specific problem your ICP already knows they have
Add a consistent CTA to every post. It does not have to be a pitch. Just a logical next step for someone who is interested.

mid.headline: You are getting traction. Now make it repeatable.
mid.text: You have proof that your content can drive real pipeline. The next step is making it predictable instead of occasional. That means a lead magnet doing its job, consistent CTAs, and content mapped to where your buyers are in the decision process.
steps: Identify your 2 or 3 highest-performing posts and figure out what made them land. Replicate that pattern.
Promote your lead magnet in your next 5 posts if you have one. Most people under-promote their best asset.
Set up a simple way to track which content is driving real conversations so you know what to do more of

high.headline: Your content is working. Now protect the system behind it.
high.text: Content that consistently builds pipeline is rare. You have built something that compounds. Each post builds authority, each lead magnet captures intent, and each conversation starts warmer because of the trust you have already built. Do not mess with what is working.
steps: Document what is working now so you can maintain it as you scale
Test new content formats or angles while keeping your proven pillars running
Look at where leads are falling off after initial interest. That is where to focus next.

questions.text: How much trust have you built with a prospect before your first outreach message lands in their inbox?

answers.label: None. I reach out cold with my offer and trust builds from there if they respond.
I personalize the message but usually get to the pitch pretty quickly.
I try to lead with value but I am not always consistent about it.
I build some context through content or a lead magnet before reaching out.
Every outreach I send is warm. They know who I am before I ever message them.

questions.text: When a prospect does not respond, what does your follow-up look like?

answers.label: I send a reminder letting them know I have not heard back.
I follow up a couple more times before giving up, usually rephrasing the same message.
I try to add value in my follow-ups but I am not always sure what to say.
I follow up with something new: a different angle, a useful resource, or a better question.
Each follow-up gives them a genuine reason to engage. If they still do not respond, I move on without guilt.

questions.text: How often do your LinkedIn conversations lead to a qualified sales meeting?

answers.label: Rarely. Most conversations go quiet before we ever get to a call.
Occasionally. Maybe one every couple of months.
Sometimes. A few per month but it is inconsistent.
Regularly. LinkedIn is a consistent source of qualified meetings for me.
LinkedIn is my primary pipeline driver. Most new meetings start here.

low.headline: Entitled follow-ups are costing you real relationships.
low.text: Your prospects do not owe you a response. Entering someone's inbox without context, then following up like they forgot to do their homework, gets you deleted. Your job is not to guilt them into acknowledging you. It is to make the conversation worth joining.
steps: Audit your last 10 outreach messages. If any of them open with what you do or what you want, rewrite them.
Before reaching out to someone, make sure they have seen your content or engaged with something you shared. Warm beats cold every single time.
Replace follow-up nudges ('just checking in', 'I have not heard back') with actual value: a useful insight, a question, a resource relevant to their situation

mid.headline: Your outreach is working. Make it warmer before you send it.
mid.text: You have figured out that value-first beats pitch-first. The next level is making sure more of your outreach goes to people who already know who you are, through your content, your lead magnets, or a shared conversation. That is when outreach stops feeling like sales and starts feeling like a natural next step.
steps: Segment your outreach list into people who know your work versus completely cold contacts. Treat them differently.
Try voice notes or video for your most important outreach. It stands out and it is harder to ignore.
Track your response rates by outreach type and double down on what is actually working

high.headline: Warm outreach at scale is your real advantage. Keep compounding it.
high.text: When trust comes first, outreach is just a conversation between two people who already understand each other. You have built that. The goal now is to keep growing the volume of warm relationships so your pipeline stays full without depending on cold volume.
steps: Map your current pipeline back to where each relationship started. It will show you where to invest more.
Systemize the move from content engagement to outreach so it happens on a schedule, not just when you remember
Protect your reply rate by never sacrificing quality for volume

questions.text: How would you describe your current LinkedIn workflow, including content creation, outreach, and follow-up?

answers.label: I do it when I have time and energy. There is no real system.
I have some routines but they fall apart when I get busy.
I have a process for some parts but not all. Content might be regular but outreach is not, or the other way around.
I have a process for most of it but I am still manually managing more than I should.
My LinkedIn system runs whether I am busy or not. Content, outreach, and follow-up all have a clear process.

questions.text: How well does your current approach connect content, outreach, and sales conversations into one system?

answers.label: They are completely disconnected. Content is one thing, outreach is another, sales is separate.
There is some connection but it is mostly coincidental.
I try to connect them but it is not consistent.
Content and outreach work together and often lead to pipeline conversations.
Content, outreach, and sales are one connected system. Each part feeds the next.

questions.text: How many hours per week do you spend on LinkedIn activities, including content creation, outreach, and follow-up combined?
questions.hint: Be honest here. A well-systemized LinkedIn workflow runs in 5 hours or less per week. Spending more than 20 hours per week suggests your process is mostly manual and disconnected.

low.headline: Without a system, LinkedIn becomes another thing that falls apart when life gets busy.
low.text: Random posting and reactive outreach can produce occasional wins, but they do not build a pipeline. Predictable results come from a predictable process. If you cannot describe exactly what happens on LinkedIn this week, this month, and next month, you do not have a system yet.
steps: Map out what a repeatable LinkedIn week looks like for you: how many posts, what kind of outreach, how you follow up
Batch your content creation. One focused session per week beats scrambling every day.
Identify the one part of your LinkedIn workflow that takes the most time and find a way to simplify it first

mid.headline: You have pieces of a system. Now wire them together.
mid.text: When content, outreach, and sales live in separate silos, you lose momentum between them. The goal is one connected process where your content warms people up, your lead magnet captures their hand-raise, and your outreach reaches them while they are already thinking about you.
steps: Draw a simple map of your current LinkedIn flow from content to conversation to call. Find where people fall out.
Create a consistent weekly routine that covers all three: content, outreach, and follow-up
Start tracking which content is driving pipeline so you stop spending time on what is not working

high.headline: You have built a system that compounds. Most people never get here.
high.text: A connected LinkedIn system where content builds trust, lead magnets capture intent, outreach starts warm conversations, and all of it feeds a repeatable pipeline, is one of the most valuable things you can build in B2B sales. Protect it.
steps: Document your system clearly enough that it could be handed off or replicated
Review it quarterly and cut anything that is taking time without producing pipeline
Look for the next constraint: is it volume, conversion, or offer? That is where to focus now.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.

computed_outputs.label: Monthly hours invested per qualified lead
